catalog_quote: In the previous literature, the Cherokee tonal and accentual system has been analyzed as a pitch-accent system (Lindsey 1987, Johnson 2005). However, after looking at the tonal and accentual phenomena in detail in this study, it is clear that the Cherokee tonal and accentual system as a whole cannot be assigned to one of the word-prosody systems in §15.1.2: it is not a canonical tonal system, nor a stress-accent system. The system as a whole can be best captured as a combinations of several systems. ... Secondly, we have seen that Superhigh Assignment (Ch.14) is best captured as a default-to-opposite accent, despite its morphosyntactic function. Cherokee superhigh accent violates Obligatoriness in (15.4), which is the definitional property of the stress-accent system according to Hyman, but it satisfies many of the ‘canonical’ features of stress-accent systems (15.5): the superhigh acce…
sweep_summary: cher1273 Cherokee is in the catalog as 'tonal' on Uchihara 2013 (held, re-read). Of the six works with stress in the title, three were held by the project and read: Uchihara 2013 (confirms; superhigh accent = default-to-opposite accent on the last non-final long vowel, else initial H4, restricted to subordinate verbs/deverbal nouns/adjectives, explicitly 'not a stress-accent system'), Cornelius 2018 (confirms; tone system + one SH pitch accent), Johnson 2005 (confirms; optional L*H accent on penult/antepenult in nouns inside a lexical-tone system). Uchihara 2016 (OUP) is paywalled (DOI 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198739449.001.0001; TOC from the OUP product page shows Ch.11 Superhigh accent, Ch.12 Typology) — low priority since the dissertation is. Wright 1996 (Cherokee Papers from UCLA, OCLC 36854333) is print-only, no online copy found (OpenLibrary no_ebook, archive.org 0 hits, UCLA page none) — medium priority as the earliest explicit accent-placement argument, but its rule ('rightmost long vowel or first syllable', p.21) is already quoted with page pins by both held dissertations. Haag 1997 (MALC proceedings, pp.343-349) is print-only with no online record; the author's own 1999 KWPL paper (downloaded open, scanned, saved) shows it concerns the word-final boundary tone and clitic attachment to the morphological word, i.e. prosody but not word stress — low priority. No item contradicts the catalog. Best first-hand statement read: Uchihara 2013 sec.14.1.1/14.1.4 pp.333/348 (same source as the catalog; does not supersede it). hunts used Crossref, Semantic Scholar (not reachable by automated download), OpenLibrary, archive.

new_statements.quote: (14.4) Superhigh Assignment (initial) Assign a superhigh accent to the last non-final long vowel of the word. [...] From the discussion in this section, it was shown that the Cherokee superhigh accent (i) is assigned to the non-final long vowel, and (ii) in the absence of a long vowel, a high tone (H4) is assigned to the first syllable of the word. Thus, it is clear that Cherokee superhigh accent resembles a default-to-opposite accent (Wright 1996: 21; Prince 1983; Hayes 1995: 296-299; Kager 1995: 384; Halle & Idsardi 1995: 412; Kager 2012), which can be formalized as an unbounded trochaic ('strong-weak') accent
new_statements.citation: Uchihara, Hiroto. 2013. Tone and Accent in Oklahoma Cherokee. PhD dissertation, University at Buffalo, SUNY (published OUP 2016).
new_statements.reading: The one stress-like element in Cherokee is a culminative superhigh pitch accent that occurs only in morphosyntactically defined word classes (subordinate verbs, deverbal nouns, adjectives) and, when present, falls on the last non-final long vowel, else (as H4) on the first syllable: a quantity-sensitive default-to-opposite accent inside a four-tone lexical tone system. Because it is not obligatory in every word, the language has no general word stress; the catalog's 'tonal' coding stands. This is the same source the catalog already relies on (sec.15.1.3); the sec.14.1.1/14.1.4 lines are a sharper placement statement from it. Independent first-hand confirmations read this search of works with stress in the title: Johnson 2005 p.16 (optional L*H accent on penult, or antepenult if the penult is short; nouns) and Cornelius 2018 p.49 (H and LF are tones, SH is a pitch accent).

new_statements.quote: Only one accent may appear per word, and in the syntactically determined forms listed above at least one accent must appear per word. Accent falls on the rightmost long vowel of a word or on the first syllable. It is characterized by a gradual rise in pitch that begins at a variable level and rises to a point above the normal high tone register and by a rise in amplitude. [...] All of these factors point to a metrically determined stress accent rather than pitch accent system. Given the distributional data, it is proposed that Cherokee has quantity sensitive unbounded feet and assigns prominence with End Rule right (ER) (Prince 1983).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tonal' coding (Wright explicitly argues Cherokee IS a tone system rather than a pitch accent system) and with the existing Uchihara 2013 statement on placement of the superhigh (last long vowel, else first syllable; culminative; restricted to subordinate verbs/deverbal nouns/adjectives): Wright 1996 is in fact the source Uchihara cites (Wright 1996:20-21) for that default-to-opposite placement. It adds first-hand phonetic detail (amplitude peak, rise above H register, 20 spectrogram tokens from speaker Virginia Carey), the metrical formalization (quantity-sensitive unbounded feet, End Rule Right, EPR/EPL), locatives as a fourth accent-bearing class, and the ty…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wright analyses Oklahoma Cherokee as a genuine tone language (lexical H vs default L, mora as tone-bearing unit, non-iterative rightward High Spread, lowfall and high-fall from laryngealization, floating H from prefixes such as distributive dee-) on top of which ONE culminative accent, the 'highrise/superhigh' (Feeling-Pulte pitch 4), is superimposed in morphosyntactically defined word classes only (verbs in subordinate clauses, deverbal nouns, locatives, most adjectives); in those forms exactly one accent per word is obligatory and its position is metrically predictable: the rightmost long vowel of the word, else (no long vowel) the first syllable = quantity-sensitive unbounded feet, End Rule Right, default-to-initial (his EPR then EPL). Because it shows an amplitude peak and overrides the syllable's tonal melody he calls it a metrically determined STRESS accent, not a pitch accent. Word-final syllables carry a predictable (upstepped) high, not marked. Words outside those classes carry tone only, no accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'Only one accent may appear per word'; no secondary or rhythmic prominence is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent is absent altogether outside the listed word classes (main-clause verbs, underived nouns etc. have tone only); when a penultimate superhigh is present the final syllable is realized as a normal high rather than the usual final superhigh/upstepped H (sec.1.2, after Feeling and Pulte); many Feeling-Pulte 'LHL' transcriptions are re-read (after Lindsey) as mistranscribed highrise accents (p.13).
new_statements.identity_note: Oklahoma (Western) Cherokee; Wright's data are primarily from one native speaker, Mrs. Virginia Carey, originally from Tahlequah, Oklahoma (UCLA field-methods consultant 1984 and 1992-93), supplemented by forms from Feeling and Pulte 1975 and Lindsey 1985/1987. The catalog record, Uchihara 2013 and this paper all describe the same variety.

tone_statements.quote: [2] represents a low level pitch and [3] a high level pitch; note that only these simple tones occur on short vowels. … we take atonic accent to be aH tone which is both [+raised peak] and [+delayed peak]. This, contra Feeling, is distinct from the H% (plus Upstep) assigned to all final vowels (when present). … Tonic accent takes the form of a mark assigned to a mora within a ‘morpheme; we take this to be a mark of the first syllable within the ‘morpheme to be assigned aH tone. tone_statements.citation: Herrick, Dylan, Marcellino Berardo, Durbin Feeling, Tracy Hirata-Edds & Lizette Peter. 2015. Collaborative Documentation and Revitalization of Cherokee Tone. Language Documentation & Conservation 9: 12-31.
tone_statements.quote: The inventory of tone is as follows: Low (represented as <a>), High (<á>), Lowfall (<àa>), and Superhigh (<aa̋>). Syllable structure is (s)C1({h/s}(C2)(h))V(:)(C3). All the data in this paper are based on Feeling‟s Cherokee-English dictionary (Feeling 1975), unless especially mentioned. … In principle, the glottal stop resulting from Laryngeal Alternation lengthens the preceding vowel (if it is a short vowel) and disappears leaving a Lowfall Tone if followed by a consonant (1a), but remains unchanged between vowels (1b).

tone_statements.summary: Four tones: Low, High, Lowfall, Superhigh; a glottal stop from laryngeal alternation drops before a consonant, lengthening the vowel and leaving a Lowfall tone. TBU, downstep, stress not treated.

tone_statements.citation: Johnson, Keith & Marcia Haag. 2005. Tone and prosodic organization in Cherokee nouns. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 117(4 Supplement): 2489. doi:10.1121/1.4809421 (ASA meeting abstract).
tone_statements.quote: Results of the ongoing project include word lists … recorded files that illustrate different tones and vowel lengths with different speakers, and a growing database containing over 1000 acoustic measurements for tone and vowel length. … The literature on Cherokee tone documents five or six surface tones (Johnson 2005; Lindsey 1985; Montgomery-Anderson 2008; Author 1975; Uchihara 2009; Wright 1996). Our findings suggest that Cherokee has a high level tone, a relatively level low tone, a low falling tone, a high falling tone, a rising tone, and a super-high tone.

tone_statements.summary: Six surface tones reported from acoustic measurements: high level, low, low falling, high falling, rising and super-high; abstract only, no statement on tone-bearing unit, downstep or word stress.

tone_statements.citation: Haag, Marcia (2002). Cherokee tone associations with overt morphology. In Chicago Linguistics Society. pp. 413–425.
tone_statements.quote: Tone in Cherokee verbs is divided into the following: (A) Tonic (A1) High Tone (represented as V´) (i) Lexical High Tone (ii) High Tone Superimposed on Verb Stem Final (iii) High Tone by Pre-Pronominal Prefix (A2) Low Tone (represented as V (without any marking)) (A3) Lowfall Tone (represented as V`) (B) Atonic (represented as V˝) … The mora is the tone-bearing unit in Cherokee (Wright 1996: 12). High Tone is the marked one as opposed to Low Tone, by the criteria proposed by Maddieson (1976: 350); High Tone is less frequent than Low Tone, and only High Tone spreads.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 43-44, Chapter 4 'Tone' (opening classification with Figure 4-1 'Realizations of Tones': High, Low, Lowfall, Superhigh (in Atonic); then 'High Tone/ Low Tone')
tone_statements.summary: Tones High, Low, Lowfall, plus a superhigh atonic accent on the rightmost long vowel of subordinate verbs, deverbal nouns, adjectives; the mora bears tone; lexical High and Lowfall derive from /ʔ/.

tone_statements.citation: Munro, Pamela. 1996. Cherokee Papers from UCLA: An Introduction. In Pamela Munro (ed.), Cherokee Papers from UCLA (UCLA Occasional Papers in Linguistics 16), 3-7. Los Angeles: UCLA Department of Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: Preliminary observations in the speech of one speaker of Cherokee led us to postulate three factors affecting tone in Cherokee. (1) Tone may be lexically specified with distinctive low, low fall, low rise, and high tones. (2) There is a metrically determined high fall pattern which may be distributed over not more than 2 syllables from the right edge of a prosodic domain. (3) Intonational domains may be associated with discourse functions, marked by high fall, or by pitch range upstep.
tone_statements.n_tones: 4 lexical (low, low fall, low rise, high) + metrical high-fall accent

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict. Wright 1996 (now read first-hand) places the single culminative 'highrise/superhigh' accent on the rightmost long vowel of the word, else on the first syllable, obligatory and unique only in subordinate-clause verbs, deverbal nouns, locatives and most adjectives, exactly the placement the catalog's existing Uchihara 2013 statement reports (Uchihara cites Wright 1996:20-21 for it); Uchihara words it 'last non-final long vowel', Wright 'rightmost long vowel' while treating the final syllable's pitch as a separate predictable boundary high, so the two pick the same vowel in practice. The only disagreement is typological labeling: Wright calls the accent a 'metrically determined stress accent' (amplitude peak, quantity-sensitive unbounded feet, End Rule Right) superimposed on a tone language, whereas Uchihara 2013 sec.15.1.3 says the system is neither canonical tone nor stress-accent and Lindsey 1987/Johnson 2005 call it pitch accent. All sources agree that tone is lexical and that there is no general word stress present in every word, so the catalog's 'tonal' coding stands; Wright's paper supports recording the restricted accent as a quantity-sensitive default-to-opposite (rightmost heavy, else initial) accent within a tone system.

sources.note: Independent second dissertation on Cherokee prosody: lexical tone (H, LF) plus one culminative, morphosyntactically restricted superhigh pitch accent placed on the rightmost long vowel (else first syllable); no obligatory word stress. Confirms the catalog's tonal coding and the superhigh placement rule.

sources.citation: Johnson, Keith. 2005. Tone and Pitch Accent in Cherokee Nouns. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 1: 1-48. doi:10.5070/P75fb5v8jb
sources.quote: Acoustic study, 4 speakers, 37 nouns: 'This acoustic phonetic study of Cherokee prosody has found that the system is a hybrid of pitch accent and lexical tone. There is an optional L*H pitch accent that is restricted to occur on the penultimate, or if the penult contains a short vowel, on the antepenultimate syllable. Three freely occurring distinctive lexical tones... two kinds of boundary tone were identified - HL% in citation forms and H% in focus construction and questions.'
sources.note: Acoustic study (4 speakers, 37 nouns): hybrid of lexical tone and an OPTIONAL, culminative L*H pitch accent (= Uchihara's superhigh) on the penult or, if the penult is short, the antepenult; absent from most monomorphemic nouns. Consistent with the catalog's tonal coding and with Uchihara's 'last non-final long vowel' rule (Johnson's data are nouns of 3-5 syllables). Not an obligatory word stress.

tone.says: Treats Cherokee as a lexical-tone language whose tone is under-documented; describes multimedia resources (pitch-contour visualisations with audio) built from phonetic documentation to train learners to perceive Cherokee tones; likely restates the tone inventory used in Herrick et al. 2015.

sources.quote: Cornelius 2018 p.45 on Wright 1996: 'the superhigh (what he calls the "high rise") is a word-level accent. He cites three factors that clearly show that this pitch is not tone ... but accent: its position is predictable (rightmost long vowel or first syllable), its starting pitch level is variable and rises to a higher point, unlike other highs in Cherokee, and it "is imposed over the existing tonal pattern, overriding the melody of the syllable on which it occurs" (Wright 1996:21). He analyzes this superhigh pitch as being the remnant of a Northern Iroquoian metrical stress system.'
sources.locator: Wright 1996: 21 as pinned by Uchihara 2013 (14.4), p.337 and p.348
sources.note: Earliest explicit argument that the superhigh is a predictable word-level accent (rightmost long vowel, else first syllable; a default-to-opposite pattern), inside a tonal system. Both held dissertations cite it with page pins (Wright 1996: 12, 13, 21) and their readings agree with the catalog's classification. sources.quote: p.36: 'what all researchers agree on is something called the boundary tone, after Lindsey (1985). tone.says: Three factors affect tone in Cherokee: (1) lexically specified tone with distinctive low, low fall, low rise and high tones; (2) a metrically determined high-fall pattern within two syllables of the right edge of a prosodic domain; (3) intonational domains marked by high fall or pitch-range upstep; analysis posits both lexical tone and metrical prosodic accent, tested on word lists and sentences from five additional speakers.

tone.quote: Tone in Cherokee verbs is divided into the following: (A) Tonic (A1) High Tone (represented as V´) (i) Lexical High Tone (ii) High Tone Superimposed on Verb Stem Final (iii) High Tone by Pre-Pronominal Prefix (A2) Low Tone (represented as V (without any marking)) (A3) Lowfall Tone (represented as V`) (B) Atonic (represented as V˝) … The mora is the tone-bearing unit in Cherokee (Wright 1996: 12). High Tone is the marked one as opposed to Low Tone, by the criteria proposed by Maddieson (1976: 350); High Tone is less frequent than Low Tone, and only High Tone spreads.
